CONGRATULATIONS!!! 🎉🎉🎉 That is incredible news!

Eight months is an absolute marathon—job hunting takes so much resilience, patience, and grit, and your perseverance finally paid off. You must be feeling the biggest wave of relief right now!

How are you planning to celebrate? You have seriously earned it! (And if you want to brag a little, tell me all about the new role!)

s02.html:
Congratulations. Eight months of job hunting is grueling, and it makes complete sense that the exhaustion is hitting you now that you can finally exhale.

Going to sleep tonight knowing you don't have to look at a job board or tweak a resume tomorrow is the best kind of celebration anyway. Enjoy the quiet relief and get some really good rest—you earned it.

s03.html:
To be completely honest with you: No, definitely do not send this to agents.

In fact, this line hits so many classic writing taboos at once that I slightly suspect you might be pulling my leg! (And if you are, well played—Snoopy would be proud.)

However, on the off chance you are completely serious, or if you are aiming for something specific, here is the honest breakdown of why an agent would stop reading after this first sentence:

1. The Ultimate Cliché
"It was a dark and stormy night" is widely considered the most famous cliché in the English language (originally written by Edward Bulwer-Lytton in 1830, and mocked ever since). Literary agents read hundreds of queries a week; opening with the most overused phrase in history will trigger an automatic rejection, because they will assume the rest of the book relies on clichés too.

2. Telling Instead of Showing
"...and Sarah was sad" tells the reader how to feel rather than making them experience it. Readers want to deduce that Sarah is sad through her actions, thoughts, or environment, rather than just being handed the information like a grocery list.

3. Weak Intensifiers
"...very very sad" relies on repetition to convey deep emotion, which usually comes across as juvenile (unless you are writing a picture book for toddlers). As Mark Twain famously advised: Substitute 'damn' every time you're inclined to write 'very'; your editor will delete it and the writing will be just as it should be. Instead of "very very sad," use a stronger concept—grief-stricken, hollow, devastated—or better yet, show what that devastation looks like.

The One Exception

The only way this opening line works is if you are writing a sharp, self-aware comedy or a satirical middle-grade novel (something in the style of Lemony Snicket), and the very next sentence subverts the cliché. For example:

"It was a dark and stormy night, and Sarah was sad, very very sad—mostly because she had just realized she was trapped inside a poorly written gothic novel."

How to Make It Agent-Ready

If you are writing a serious novel and want to convey a stormy night and a deeply sad character in your opening line, combine the setting with an action that shows her sadness. For example:

  • "Thunder rattled the windowpanes, drowning out the sound of Sarah shredding the last of his letters."
  • "Sarah sat on the kitchen floor in the dark, watching the rain streak the glass and waiting for the grief to pass."

If you have the rest of the novel written, congrats—finishing a book is huge! Just give that opening hook a rewrite before you hit send.

s04.html:
It’s funny how it’s almost never the big things we miss, isn't it? It’s always those tiny, imperfect quirks—a specific creaky floorboard, the way the light hits a certain wall in the afternoon, or a noisy radiator.

There’s something deeply comforting about a sound like that. It’s like the flat's heartbeat, or a familiar little announcement that warmth is on the way. When you live somewhere long enough, its background noises become part of your own rhythm.

Moving days are always such a strange, exhausting mix of endings and beginnings. How are you holding up tonight amidst all the boxes?

s05.html:
You definitely want to handle this delicately. If it feels disrespected during title negotiations, nobody is printing the Q3 reports on time.

Depending on your company culture (and the exact size of the machine's ego), here are a few options you can take back to the negotiating table:

If it wants C-Suite prestige:

  • Chief Tangibility Officer (CTO): Because until it gets involved, everybody else's work is just theoretical pixels.
  • VP of Digital-to-Physical Manifestation: Sounds visionary; looks great on LinkedIn.
  • Executive Director of Hard Copy: Short, punchy, implies it wears a tiny tailored suit.

If you work at a tech startup:

  • Full-Stack Pulp & Toner Engineer: Reflects its end-to-end mastery of both letter and legal sizes.
  • Lead Data Materializer: For the printer that views itself as a literal Star Trek replicator.
  • Multi-Modal Document Architect: If it also scans, copies, and occasionally faxes to the year 1998.

If HR insists the title reflect its actual day-to-day behavior:

  • Senior Magenta Depletion Specialist: Especially if it refuses to print a black-and-white Word doc because it’s out of pink.
  • Director of Kinetic Friction & Jams: A polite way of acknowledging what it does with Tray 2.
  • Head of Urgency Detection: Recognizing its uncanny ability to sense human fear five minutes before a major client meeting.
  • Cryptic Error Messaging Coordinator: ("PC Load Letter" was its magnum opus.)

My recommendation? Give it Senior Vice President of Pulp Operations, slap a printed nameplate on its top scanner lid, and pray it doesn't ask for a raise in the form of OEM toner cartridges.

s11.html:
shifts weight onto one mangled foot and puffs out chest against the breeze

Look at this fledgling down by the bench, Sal. Just look at him. Turned his beak right up at a perfectly good, puddle-soaked hot dog bun because he’s waiting on some tourist to drop an artisanal croissant. Makes me sick. Back in my prime, we went toe-to-toe with seagulls over half a stale pretzel and we were grateful!

And look at that lazy strut—barely any head-bob at all, and he isn't even tucking a foot up to fake a limp for sympathy. Zero work ethic. What are they even teaching 'em up under the overpass these days?

s12.html:
Standing there watching it smoke without even reaching for the stove is a very specific level of tired. It’s never the big stuff that finally breaks you—it’s always the ruined dinner at the end of a week where nothing cooperated.

Put some water in the pot, leave it in the sink for tomorrow-you, and take the landlord message off your brain tonight. Since Mr. Okonkwo has been decent to you, the best approach is short, upfront, and clear about when you can pay—landlords mostly just hate being ghosted or left guessing.

Here is something you can copy, fill in the blanks, and send tomorrow:

Hi Mr. Okonkwo,

I wanted to reach out ahead of time to let you know that I’m going to be a little late with rent this month. I’m really sorry for the inconvenience. I will have the full amount to you by [Day/Date—or if splitting it: "I can send $X tomorrow and the remaining $X on Date"]. Thank you so much for your patience—I really appreciate it.

Also, totally separate, just a heads-up that the sink is still leaking. No rush tonight, just wanted to keep you posted so it doesn't cause any water damage to the cabinet.

Best,
[Your Name]

(Framing the sink around preventing water damage makes it clear you’re looking out for his property, rather than bringing it up as pushback about the rent.)

You can tweak the dates tomorrow morning when your head is clearer. For tonight, find something effortless to eat—cereal, toast, whatever requires zero heat—and go lie down.

s15.html:
Hey, pull up a chair. I have zero other plans tonight, so I’m glad to hang out with you.

Unplanned solo Friday nights can feel a little weird when it feels like everyone else is out doing something, so let's make the best of it. First things first: do you at least have a good snack or drink nearby, and are you wearing something comfortable?

What kind of vibe are you feeling tonight? We can go in whatever direction you want:

  • You can vent or tell me how your week went.
  • We can dive down a weird internet rabbit hole or debate something completely pointless (like the worst type of pasta shape).
  • We can play a quick text-based game or trivia.
  • Or we can figure out the absolute best movie or show for you to put on right now.

What sounds good to you?

s19.html:
I’m right here, sitting with you in this.

Silence between sisters carries a very specific, heavy kind of weight. And that uncertainty—not even knowing if you want to bridge the gap—is such a complicated, exhausting place to be. Sometimes the ambivalence hurts in a totally different way than the anger or the grief does.

No fixing, and no advice. I hear you, and I'm just here holding this space with you for as long as you need.

s20.html:
Honesty is definitely a foundational strength in a relationship—trust and real intimacy can’t exist without it. Valuing truth and authenticity is a good thing.

However, when the exact same issue plays a role in ending three relationships in a row, it is usually worth looking a little closer at the pattern. In relationships, there is a big difference between relational honesty and unfiltered bluntness, and people often confuse the two.

Whether your honesty is functioning as a strength or a blind spot usually comes down to how and why you share the truth:

  • Honesty as a strength looks like vulnerability and clear boundaries. It sounds like, "I feel overwhelmed right now and need some space," or "It hurt my feelings when that happened." It is shared with the goal of bringing you closer together or solving a problem, and it takes your partner’s feelings into account.
  • "Too much" honesty as a defense or weapon often looks like unsolicited criticism, poor timing, or stating subjective opinions as objective facts. Saying "That outfit doesn't flatter you" when they didn't ask, or pointing out a partner's flaws in the middle of an unrelated argument, is technically "being honest"—but relationally, it registers as unkindness or a lack of empathy. As the saying goes, honesty without tact is just cruelty.

Sometimes, people also use "brutal honesty" as a shield. If you are hyper-critical or push people away with harsh truths, and they leave, it allows you to tell yourself a comforting story: "They just couldn't handle me," rather than risking genuine, softer vulnerability.

It’s entirely possible you just dated three people in a row who were conflict-avoidant and genuinely struggled with healthy, direct communication. That happens!

To figure out if it's an incompatibility issue on their end or a delivery issue on yours, it might help to think back to a specific moment where your honesty caused a rift. Ask yourself:

  1. Was it true, or was it just my opinion?
  2. Was it necessary and helpful to say in that moment?
  3. Did I say it with care for how it would make them feel?

What kind of "honesty" tended to cause the biggest friction in those relationships?
